title: 2 Samuel 9:9–13
context: David puts the arrangement into effect. He gives Saul’s estate to Mephibosheth and assigns Ziba, with his fifteen sons and twenty servants, to farm it, while Mephibosheth eats at the king’s table like one of the king’s sons. The chapter closes by noting his young son Mica, his home in Jerusalem, and, once more, that he was lame in both feet. Many readers in both traditions see in the scene a picture of grace shown to the undeserving for another’s sake.

verses.text: Then the king called to Ziba, Saul’s servant, and said to him, “All that belonged to Saul and to all his house I have given to your master’s son.
verses.arminianNotes: David tells Ziba that all of Saul’s property now belongs to his master’s son. Arminian readers note that the king formalizes his promise, making it public and binding before the servant who managed the household.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the transfer as a concrete expression of covenant faithfulness, not merely words of goodwill. Shared ground: the verse makes David’s kindness practical, giving Mephibosheth a real inheritance to support his household.

verses.text: Till the land for him—you, your sons, and your servants. Bring in the harvest, that your master’s son may have bread to eat; but Mephibosheth your master’s son will always eat bread at my table.” Now Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants.
verses.arminianNotes: Ziba, his sons, and servants are to farm the land for Mephibosheth, while he eats at the king’s table. Arminian readers note the careful arrangement, ensuring both an income for his household and a place of honor at court.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the size of Ziba’s household, fifteen sons and twenty servants, showing a substantial estate. Both traditions read the verse as David providing for Mephibosheth’s needs fully, not leaving him dependent on chance.

verses.text: Then Ziba said to the king, “According to all that my lord the king commands his servant, so your servant will do.” So Mephibosheth ate at the king’s table like one of the king’s sons.
verses.arminianNotes: Ziba agrees to do all that the king commands, and Mephibosheth eats at the table like one of the king’s sons. Arminian readers see the striking image of a former rival’s grandson treated as part of the royal family.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the phrase “like one of the king’s sons” a picture many apply to adoption into God’s family. Shared ground: both traditions draw on the image as an illustration of grace, while reading the verse first as history.

verses.text: Mephibosheth had a young son, whose name was Mica. All who lived in Ziba’s house were servants to Mephibosheth.
verses.arminianNotes: Mephibosheth has a young son named Mica, and Ziba’s household serves him. Arminian readers note that the line of Jonathan continues, and that Mica’s descendants are later listed in 1 Chronicles 8:34–35.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see David’s kindness extending to the next generation, as the covenant with Jonathan had requested (1 Samuel 20:15). Both traditions read the mention of Mica as showing that the kindness had lasting effects for Jonathan’s family.

verses.text: So Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, for he ate continually at the king’s table. He was lame in both his feet.
verses.arminianNotes: Mephibosheth lives in Jerusalem and eats at the king’s table, lame in both feet. Arminian readers note that the chapter ends by repeating his disability, which reminds readers that the kindness was not based on what he could offer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the closing note as underscoring grace given to one who could not earn it. Shared ground: the repetition of his lameness frames the whole story, and both traditions read it as highlighting the generosity of David’s covenant faithfulness.
